title: Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?
text:
- 1. The context While this was in part covered by the first report, Milburn is at pains to begin the new volume with his belief that the issue of Neets is not a failure of the younger generation but a case of them being let down by a series of structural factors. “The young people I have met over the last year are not asking for an easier life. They are asking for a fair chance to build one,” he writes. The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.” At the centre of the proposed new system is a youth opportunity service (YOS), which would offer young people support in areas such as training and health – and would in return expect participation.
- 2. The goals Currently, about 13.5% of people aged 16-24 in the UK are classified as Neet, the highest proportion in Europe outside Romania. This is not a new problem, the report notes, pointing out that the Neet rate has stayed above 10% for most of the past 25 years. The aim over a decade-long transformational plan would be to match the records of the best-performing European nations on this metric, such as the Netherlands and Denmark. While Milburn talks playfully of aiming for “Neet zero”, he says this means an eventual consistent rate of about 5%. He says the policies in his plan would get the Neet rate to about 6.8% by 2036.
- 3. Employers and the labour market Noting that youth employment has declined even as overall employment rose, Milburn says opportunities are limited by issues affecting young people – for example, a lack of connections to secure work experience or first jobs – and also employers, including the costs of taking on staff and regulatory complexities. The report says this is worsened by a lack of government help. While Denmark spends about 1% of GDP on all-age hiring incentives and subsidies, in the UK it is about 0.1%. The report sets out a series of recommendations, including: 
 
  - Doubling the salary threshold for employer national insurance for entry-level jobs for young people in retail and hospitality, possibly then expanded to other sectors.
  - Extending the existing youth jobs grant, which gives up to £3,000 to employers who takes on a staff member on universal credit for at least six months, so it also applies to people not on benefits, with extra incentives for small employers and people facing barriers, such as those with disabilities or care leavers.
  - Avoid minimum pay rates being a barrier – for example, any moves to put young people’s minimum wages closer the adult rate should be judged “against the critical goal of protecting youth employment”.
  - This should be matched with increased simplicity for companies, with a single digital gateway leading to all the schemes set up to help young workers, and more clarity on help for workers with disabilities.
All this would be united in a so-called youth opportunity test, under which any future tax or regulatory policy changes would look at their effect on young workers, set out in a law.
- 4. Education and training The report notes that this is a long-term issue, with many of the indicators of future Neet status, such as low attainment and poor attendance, being clear during childhood. Milburn also says that while countries with low Neet rates take vocational skills seriously, in England “technical education has too often been regarded as for somebody else’s child”. Among changes the report recommends are: 
 
  - More investment in early years provision, such as family hubs, and individual support in school if a student is seen as being at “material risk of disengagement”.
  - Less use of school exclusion where possible. The report notes that the Netherlands has a permanent exclusion rate 73% lower than England’s.
  - More focus in school on preparedness for work, as well as passing exams.
  - More investment in further education and in apprenticeships, with greater financial incentives for employers who hire apprentices.
  - University courses “must be able to demonstrate clear value for learners, employers and the wider economy,” with funding withdrawn for poorly performing examples.
- 5. Health The report identifies health as central to the Neets issue, with more than half of young people in this position reporting a health condition. Milburn says much of this is down to a health service “designed to diagnose and treat illness” rather than intervening earlier, and that is not aimed at helping people into work, with diagnoses and the fit note system creating a “binary” mindset. It recommends: 
 
  - Much quicker access to health and mental health assistance, long before a formal diagnosis, based around the new YOS system. If someone has a health issue, their YOS-designated adviser can point them towards advice and help, potentially including talking therapies.
  - A move away from GPs issuing fit notes, which would instead become the responsibility of other health experts such as occupational therapists or non-clinicians such as employment advisers.
- 6. Social security The report is highly critical of what it calls a current system that can trap people in dependence. “It asks a young person what they cannot do before it asks them what, with the right support, they could. The welfare system for too many young people has become a trap when it ought to be a springboard.” At the same time, it argues that crudely cutting rates or entitlement do not work, “fiscally nor morally”. It says: “If they leave young people destitute, then costs merely show up somewhere else on the state’s balance sheet in health, housing or criminal justice. Spending less is not the same as succeeding. The test is whether lives and trajectories change.” Saying more must be invested in helping people on benefits, it recommends: 
 
  - A new “opportunity guarantee” for a place in education, training or work for anyone aged 18 to 24, along with a “support guarantee” for the support required for them to do this. Based on significant investment, these must be in place before the changes begin, the report says.
  - Among the options under the guarantee are: a government-subsidised job with employers receiving £3,000 for each young person they recruit – more for smaller businesses or when the employee has extra needs; an FE place, or technical or university learning as appropriate; an apprenticeship; a work placement of up to 12 weeks; structured volunteering such as conservation, community gardening or a cadetship; help to create a business.
  - The “backstop” to all this would be a state-financed six-month job with an employer.
  - The creation of a new “youth allowance”, set at the under-25 rate of universal credit.
  - A new “health and disability fund” operated by the local YOS to help with extra costs, which are or might be time-limited.
  - An “additional cost allowance”, replacing personal independence payment for young people, when their disability-related extra costs “are significant, established and ongoing”. The report says eligibility “would be more closely targeted at those with demonstrable extra costs for functional needs that are long-term and enduring”, with an aim of enabling independence and participation.
  - A “severe and complex needs insurance”, a more generous long-term award without a qualifying period, for those with the most profound disabilities, and where it is clear they are unlikely ever to be able to work.
  - With this would come changes to “actively reward and enable participation”, for example allowing young people to keep more earnings before benefits are cut, and extra money for people who undertake civic service.
  - With this would come a responsibility to engage. Someone who persistently refuses to do so would lose their youth allowance benefit, but only after “multiple attempts to re-engage and understand what has gone wrong”.
- 7. The costs While much of the media buildup to the report has been questions about whether the changes could result in benefits payments overall starting to fall in this parliament, Milburn makes it plain that this must be a longer-term process, with investment preceding savings. The report says: “While the intention is to hit the ground running, the speed of change has to be sustained over time. This is a 10-year plan, not a one-year sprint … Short-termism has been a constant feature of our country’s approach to this issue over the last 50 years.” This would involve an initial investment of £500m in 2027-28, taken from existing spending, which would then “ramp up”. By 2036-37, the report says, annual investment would be about £5.8bn, covering the guarantees, hiring incentives and health, education and skills changes, offset by £3.6bn of savings and £2.4bn in increased tax revenues, covering lower welfare payments and more tax receipts.
